header: V e r s u s.
Present: Mr. Fazalullah Khan, Advocate for petitioners.
Sardar Aman Khan, Advocate for respondent No. 1.
J U D G M E N T
body: SYED MUDASSER AMEER, J. – Through this civil revision petition filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the petitioners have challenged the judgment and decree dated 09.02.2010, passed by the learned District Judge, Abbottabad, whereby their appeal against the judgment and decree dated 17.06.2009, passed by the learned Civil Judge, Abbottabad, in two consolidated suits, was dismissed. Through the said judgment, the learned trial Court had dismissed Civil Suit No.208/1 of 1994, instituted by Nazir Ahmad Abbasi (since deceased) through his legal heirs, and decreed Civil Suit No.209/1 of 1996, instituted by respondent Muhammad Ibrahim for recovery of possession of the disputed house. The petitioners seek setting aside of the judgments and decrees of the courts below and acceptance of their suit.

2. Briefly stated, the dispute concerns a residential house situated at Lambi Dheri, Abbottabad, comprising property falling in Khasra Nos.782 and 783. The predecessor of the petitioners, Nazir Ahmad Abbasi, and respondent Muhammad Ibrahim had certain financial dealings. The respondent claimed that he had advanced an amount of Rs.434,000/- to Nazir Ahmad Abbasi in connection with the proposed purchase of a plot measuring one kanal on Kakul Road, which was not subsequently transferred. According to the respondent, an outstanding liability consequently arose against Nazir Ahmad Abbasi.

3. On 10.03.1992, the parties executed a written agreement concerning the house in question. Under its terms, if the outstanding debt was not discharged by 10.06.1992, Nazir Ahmad Abbasi would transfer his house to Muhammad Ibrahim. The stipulated date passed without settlement of the liability. Thereafter, on 21.06.1992, stamp papers were purchased and a separate sale deed in respect of the house was prepared. Before its registration, however, Nazir Ahmad Abbasi backed out of the transaction. He maintained that the debt, or a substantial portion thereof, had been cleared and that another agreement dated 27.07.1992 had subsequently been executed. The respondent disputes that version.

4. The subsequent registration proceedings are material. On 19.07.1992, Muhammad Ibrahim approached the Sub-Registrar, Abbottabad, seeking compulsory registration of the proposed sale deed dated 21.06.1992. Upon refusal, he approached the District Registrar on 22.08.1992. The District Registrar, through order/letter dated 18.10.1992, declined the requested relief. He recorded that Nazir Ahmad Abbasi had obtained a refund voucher against the stamp papers relating to the sale deed and had encashed the amount from the Treasury. Muhammad Ibrahim was accordingly advised to seek his remedy before the civil Court.

5. Having failed to secure registration of the separate sale deed, Muhammad Ibrahim, on 16.12.1992, applied to the Sub- Registrar for compulsory registration of the earlier agreement dated 10.03.1992. The Sub-Registrar refused registration vide order dated 13.02.1993, recorded on the reverse of the agreement. Muhammad Ibrahim challenged that refusal before the District Registrar. The appeal, dated 06.03.1993, was accepted vide order dated 02.03.1994, whereby the District Registrar directed compulsory registration of the agreement dated 10.03.1992. Pursuant thereto, the document was registered on 09.03.1994.

6. Nazir Ahmad Abbasi challenged the order of the District Registrar dated 02.03.1994 by instituting Civil Suit No.208/1 of 1994, seeking declaration that the said order was illegal, without lawful authority and ineffective to transfer ownership of the house. During pendency of the suit, he died and his legal heirs were brought on record. On the other hand, Muhammad Ibrahim instituted Civil Suit No.209/1 of 1996, seeking possession of the house on the assertion that ownership had passed to him through compulsory registration of the agreement dated 10.03.1992.

7. Both suits were consolidated. The learned trial Court, vide judgment and decree dated 17.06.2009, dismissed the suit of Nazir Ahmad Abbasi and decreed the suit of Muhammad Ibrahim. The learned District Judge, Abbottabad, maintained that decision through judgment dated 09.02.2010. Hence, the instant revision petition.
8. Arguments heard. Record perused.

9. The controversy raises two fundamental questions: first, whether the instrument dated 10.03.1992, by its terms, transferred ownership of the house to Muhammad Ibrahim or merely embodied an agreement for its future transfer; and secondly, whether the District Registrar lawfully directed its compulsory registration vide order dated 02.03.1994.
Legal character of the agreement dated 10.03.1992 10. The first question goes to the root of the controversy and is decisive of the respondent's claim for possession.

11. The relevant stipulation in the agreement dated 10.03.1992 was that, in the event of failure to discharge the outstanding debt by 10.06.1992, Nazir Ahmad Abbasi would transfer his house to Muhammad Ibrahim. The language and substance of the stipulation are significant. It did not declare that the house stood sold or that ownership was being transferred immediately. It imposed an obligation upon Nazir Ahmad Abbasi to transfer the property in future upon the occurrence of a specified contingency.

12. The distinction between a sale and an agreement to sell is fundamental. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 defines a sale as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised, or part-paid and part-promised. It further provides that a contract for sale is an agreement that a sale shall take place on terms settled between the parties and that such a contract does not, of itself, create any interest in or charge upon the property.

13. Thus, an agreement to sell, however clearly executed or acknowledged, is not itself a conveyance. It creates a contractual right to obtain another document which will transfer title. It does not make the prospective purchaser the owner.

14. The august Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed this principle. In Hakim Ali and another v. Atta Muhammad and another (1981 SCMR 993), the Supreme Court held that an agreement contemplating transfer of immovable property in future does not, by itself, transfer or charge any existing interest in the property.

15. In Mst. Rasheeda Begum and others v. Muhammad Yousaf and others (2002 SCMR 1089), the Court explained that an agreement to sell creates a right to obtain another document conferring title, but does not itself create an interest or charge in the property.

16. Likewise, in Shah Muhammad v. Atta Muhammad (2005 SCMR 969), it was held in clear terms that an agreement to sell is not a document of title and cannot form the basis for a declaratory decree under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877.

17. The same principle was reiterated in Muhammad Iqbal and others v. Mst. Baseerat and others (2017 SCMR 367). The Supreme Court upheld interference in revisional jurisdiction where the courts below had conferred ownership on the basis of an agreement to sell, holding that the issue concerned the correct application of law rather than mere appreciation of evidence.

18. These authorities apply directly. The agreement dated 10.03.1992 was, at most, a contract for transfer of the house in future if the outstanding liability remained unpaid. It did not transfer ownership to Muhammad Ibrahim.

The subsequent proposed sale deed dated 21.06.1992 19. The subsequent conduct of the parties further confirms this interpretation. When the debt was not discharged by 10.06.1992, the parties proceeded to prepare a separate sale deed dated 21.06.1992. Stamp papers were purchased and a distinct instrument was drawn up for the transfer of the house. Muhammad Ibrahim himself approached the registration authorities seeking compulsory registration of that sale deed.

20. Had ownership already passed under the agreement dated 10.03.1992, there would have been no occasion to prepare another sale deed in respect of the same property or to seek its compulsory registration. This subsequent conduct is not being considered to vary the terms of the March agreement. It is relevant to ascertain the nature of the transaction which the parties themselves understood to have taken place. It confirms that the March agreement contemplated a future conveyance rather than an immediate transfer of ownership.

21. The separate sale deed dated 21.06.1992 was never registered. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 requires a registered instrument for transfer of immovable property of the prescribed value. Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 also prevents an instrument required to be registered from operating to create or transfer title unless registered. Consequently, the June instrument did not transfer ownership either.
22. The respondent's attempt to obtain registration of that instrument failed, and the District Registrar, through order dated 18.10.1992, advised him to pursue his remedy before the civil Court.

23. The order dated 18.10.1992 deserves separate mention. It concerned the distinct sale deed dated 21.06.1992 and the application made for its compulsory registration. It was not an adjudication of the subsequent application concerning the agreement dated 10.03.1992. Therefore, the earlier order cannot, by itself, be treated as res judicata or as a statutory bar against proceedings concerning the March agreement. Both were separate instruments and the applications related to different documents.

24. Nevertheless, the sequence is significant. It demonstrates that the parties treated the June instrument as the sale deed required to effect transfer of ownership, while the March instrument remained the underlying agreement for a future transfer. The failure of the June deed to obtain registration could not convert the earlier agreement into an absolute sale.

The subsequent agreement dated 27.07.1992 and payment of money 25. The courts below placed considerable reliance upon the payment of money by Muhammad Ibrahim to Nazir Ahmad Abbasi. The appellate Court also found that, although the alleged joint property business had not been satisfactorily proved, there was independent evidence of payment through receipts and a bank draft.

26. There is no necessity to disturb those factual findings. Even if it is accepted that Muhammad Ibrahim advanced the amount claimed by him and that some liability remained outstanding, the legal consequence is not that ownership of the house automatically passed to him. Payment of money may establish a debt, advance, earnest payment or contractual liability. Its character depends upon the transaction to which it relates. Proof of payment cannot substitute a conveyance.

27. The parties also relied upon a subsequent agreement dated 27.07.1992. The petitioners maintained that the accounts had been settled or the earlier arrangement modified, whereas the respondent disputed the alleged cancellation. The courts below were not persuaded that the later agreement had cancelled the earlier arrangement and treated it as a continuation of the financial dealings between the parties.

28. Even accepting that factual conclusion in favour of the respondent, it does not advance his claim to ownership. The subsequent document, as discussed by the trial Court, provided a right to recover the outstanding amount from the person or property of Nazir Ahmad Abbasi. It did not itself execute a conveyance of the house or declare that ownership had already vested in Muhammad Ibrahim.

29. The question whether the July agreement superseded or continued the March agreement, therefore, need not be finally resolved. Even if the March agreement remained operative and the debt was not discharged, it created, at most, a contractual right to demand a future transfer. It did not confer present ownership.

30. Nor can the March agreement be treated as a mortgage by conditional sale merely because it arose out of a debt. Section 58(c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 contemplates an ostensible present sale of the property, subject to a condition that the sale shall become absolute upon default, or become void, or be followed by retransfer upon payment. The condition must be embodied in the document which effects or purports to effect the sale.

31. In Abdul Sattar v. Sardar Begum (1992 SCMR 417), the Supreme Court examined the distinction between an agreement to sell and a mortgage by conditional sale and emphasized that the real character of the transaction must be determined in accordance with section 58(c).

32. The instrument before us did not purport to effect an ostensible sale in the present. It stipulated that Nazir Ahmad Abbasi would transfer the house in future if the debt remained unpaid by the specified date. No present conveyance was made. Nor does the document establish a presently created mortgage interest which could entitle the respondent to claim possession as absolute owner. At most, it embodied a contractual security arrangement, the enforcement of which had to be pursued through the remedies recognized by law.

Legality of the compulsory registration order dated 02.03.1994 33. There is another independent defect in the respondent's claim. The compulsory registration proceedings concerning the agreement dated 10.03.1992 were not in accordance with the time prescribed by the Registration Act, 1908.

34. Section 23 of the Act provides that no document, other than a will, shall be accepted for registration unless presented to the proper registering officer within four months from the date of its execution, subject to the exceptions contained in sections 24, 25 and

26. 35. Section 25 provides a limited extension where a document could not be presented within the prescribed period owing to urgent necessity or unavoidable accident. The Registrar may, in such circumstances, direct acceptance of the document where the delay does not exceed a further four months, subject to payment of a fine not exceeding ten times the proper registration fee.
36. The statutory extension is not unlimited. It does not authorize registration whenever a party chooses to approach the registering authority, irrespective of the lapse of time.

37. In the present case, the agreement was executed on 10.03.1992. The ordinary four-month period under section 23 expired on 10.07.1992. Even if the respondent could have established urgent necessity or unavoidable accident under section 25, the additional period of four months would have expired on 10.11.1992.

38. The respondent did not apply for registration of this agreement on 19.07.1992. That application related to the separate sale deed dated 21.06.1992. The first application seeking compulsory registration of the agreement dated 10.03.1992 was made on 16.12.1992. It was, therefore, presented after expiry of both the ordinary period under section 23 and the maximum permissible extension under section 25.

39. No material has been identified showing that the respondent sought or obtained a valid extension under section 25, established urgent necessity or unavoidable accident, or paid the fine prescribed by that provision. The District Registrar, in his order dated 02.03.1994, did not address this statutory impediment. He merely observed that the document had been signed by Nazir Ahmad Abbasi, attested by marginal witnesses and that the necessary formalities had been complied with.

40. Proof of execution could not dispense with the mandatory time requirement. The Registrar's power to direct registration under section 72 or section 75 was subject to compliance with the other provisions of the Act, including sections 23 and 25.

41. It is correct that the respondent appealed against the Sub- Registrar's refusal dated 13.02.1993 on 06.03.1993, apparently within the thirty-day period prescribed by section 72. The document was also registered on 09.03.1994, within thirty days of the District Registrar's order dated 02.03.1994, as contemplated by section 72(2).

42. These subsequent steps, however, do not cure the original defect. The statutory period for initial presentation had already expired beyond the maximum extension permitted by section 25. The appeal and the subsequent act of registration could not retrospectively confer upon the Registrar a power which the Act did not provide.

43. The order dated 02.03.1994 was, therefore, passed without lawful compliance with the mandatory requirements governing presentation of documents. The consequential registration dated 09.03.1994 cannot provide a lawful foundation for transfer of title.

44. There is a further distinction which must be maintained. The earlier order dated 18.10.1992 concerned the separate sale deed dated 21.06.1992. It did not finally determine the later application concerning the March agreement. Thus, the illegality of the order dated 02.03.1994 does not rest merely upon the fact that the District Registrar had earlier declined to direct registration of another document.

45. The decisive defect is that the March agreement was presented for the first time on 16.12.1992, beyond the period prescribed by sections 23 and 25. The District Registrar could not disregard that statutory bar simply because execution of the document was admitted.

The respondent's entitlement to possession 46. The respondent instituted Civil Suit No.209/1 of 1996 seeking possession on the assertion that he had become owner through compulsory registration of the agreement dated 10.03.1992. That foundation is legally unsustainable.

47. A registered agreement to sell does not become a sale deed merely because it has been entered in the registration record. Registration authenticates the document and gives it only such legal effect as its contents and the law permit. It cannot convert a agreement for future transfer into an immediate conveyance of ownership.

48. In Muhammad Iqbal and others v. Mst. Baseerat and others (2017 SCMR 367), the Supreme Court specifically held that an agreement to sell does not confer title under section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, read with section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908. The Court further held that interference in revisional jurisdiction was justified where the courts below had granted ownership on the basis of an agreement to sell, as the controversy involved the correct application of law.

49. Similarly, in Sh. Manzoor Ahmad and others v. Mst. Iqbal Begum and others (1989 SCMR 949), the Supreme Court explained that section 53-A of the Transfer of Property Act protects possession in part performance. It does not confer ownership or provide an independent right to obtain possession upon a prospective purchaser who has not already taken possession in part performance.

50. The respondent did not establish possession under the March agreement and then seek protection against dispossession. He instituted a suit to obtain possession on the assertion that ownership had already passed to him. Section 53-A cannot support such a claim.

51. The appropriate remedy for enforcing an agreement to sell is a suit for specific performance, subject to proof of the contract, performance of the plaintiff's obligations and limitation. Article 113 of the Limitation Act, 1908 prescribes three years for such a suit, commencing from the date fixed for performance or, where no date is fixed, from the date when the plaintiff has notice that performance is refused.
52. In Muhammad Ramzan v. Muhammad Qasim (2011 SCMR 249), the Supreme Court explained that where a date is fixed for performance, the three-year period under Article 113 runs from that date.

53. Here, the obligation to transfer the house was stipulated to arise upon failure to discharge the debt by 10.06.1992. Any claim for specific performance on that basis had to be pursued within three years from the stipulated date. The period expired on 10.06.1995. The respondent instituted his suit for possession on 31.03.1996, after expiry of that period. More importantly, he did not seek specific performance; his claim was founded upon an assertion of existing ownership through compulsory registration.
54. He cannot obtain, through a suit for possession as owner, the very transfer which the agreement contemplated for the future and which required enforcement through the remedy provided by law.

55. This Court is not required to determine whether the respondent is entitled to recover any amount allegedly advanced by him to Nazir Ahmad Abbasi. Nor is it necessary to decide the precise state of accounts between the parties. Any independent monetary claim or legally enforceable security, if available, remains subject to the law of limitation and all other defences. The present proceedings determine only that the respondent did not acquire ownership of the house through the agreement dated 10.03.1992 or its subsequent compulsory registration.

Revisional jurisdiction and final determination 56. Ordinarily, concurrent findings of fact are not disturbed in revision under section 115 CPC. But this rule does not protect a judgment founded upon an incorrect application of law or an erroneous legal construction of the document on which the decree rests.

57. The material factual findings need not be disturbed. It may be accepted that Nazir Ahmad Abbasi executed the agreement dated 10.03.1992, that Muhammad Ibrahim advanced money to him, that the parties subsequently prepared a separate sale deed dated 21.06.1992 and that another agreement dated 27.07.1992 was brought into existence. The question is what legal consequences flow from these facts.

58. The courts below treated the March agreement as a completed sale merely because it was executed, subsequently registered and supported by evidence of payment. They failed to examine its operative terms and to distinguish a promise to transfer property in future from a present conveyance. They also failed to consider the statutory time requirements governing its registration.

59. These are errors of law going to the foundation of the decree for possession. In Muhammad Iqbal (2017 SCMR 367), the Supreme Court recognised that such an error is amenable to correction in revisional jurisdiction and does not amount to impermissible reappraisal of evidence.

60. There is no justification for remanding the matter. The dispute is more than three decades old and this revision has remained pending since 2010. The record further shows that after framing of issues on 06.05.2009, learned counsel for both sides made joint statements that they would rely upon the evidence already recorded and did not wish to produce any further evidence.

61. The parties have had ample opportunity to establish their respective cases. The respondent had to prove that ownership had passed to him. The petitioners had to establish the grounds upon which they challenged compulsory registration. Neither side should now be afforded another opportunity to fill deficiencies in its evidence. More importantly, the decisive questions are legal and can be determined on the existing record.

62. For the foregoing reasons, this civil revision petition is allowed. The judgment and decree dated 09.02.2010, passed by the learned District Judge, Abbottabad, and the consolidated judgment and decree dated 17.06.2009, passed by the learned Civil Judge, Abbottabad, are set aside.
63. Consequently:

(i) Civil Suit No.208/1 of 1994, instituted by Nazir Ahmad Abbasi (since deceased) through his legal heirs, is decreed. The order dated 02.03.1994, passed by the District Registrar, Abbottabad, directing compulsory registration of the agreement dated 10.03.1992, is declared illegal and without lawful authority for want of compliance with sections 23 and 25 of the Registration Act, 1908, and is accordingly set aside. The consequential registration dated 09.03.1994 shall not operate to confer any title or proprietary interest upon Muhammad Ibrahim.

(ii) It is declared that the instrument dated 10.03.1992 was an agreement for future transfer of the house upon failure to discharge the stipulated liability. It was not an absolute sale deed and did not, by itself, transfer ownership to Muhammad Ibrahim. The ownership of the disputed property, therefore, remained with Nazir Ahmad Abbasi and devolved upon his legal heirs in accordance with law. (iii) Civil Suit No.209/1 of 1996, instituted by Muhammad Ibrahim for recovery of possession of the house on the basis of the alleged ownership acquired through the compulsory registration of the agreement dated 10.03.1992, is dismissed.

(iv) It is clarified that nothing in this judgment shall be construed as a finding that Muhammad Ibrahim did not advance money to Nazir Ahmad Abbasi or has no independent monetary claim against his estate. Any such claim shall remain subject to limitation and all other defences available under the law.
64. The parties shall bear their own costs.
Announced.
J U D G E
